body:
Why Indian passengers were refused entry to Canada

The Komagata Maru incident of 1914 concerned a ship carrying Indian migrants who sought admission to Canada. Many people from Punjab had travelled overseas for work, but Canadian immigration policy placed discriminatory barriers before Asian migrants. A 1908 continuous journey regulation required immigrants to travel directly from their country of origin without stopping en route. Regular direct sea passages from India to Canada were effectively unavailable, making this condition an obstacle to Indian migration.

Gurdit Singh, an Indian businessman, chartered the Japanese steamship Komagata Maru to challenge these restrictions and take Indian passengers to Canada. The undertaking was an immigration challenge, even though it later became closely connected with anti-colonial nationalism.

The voyage and its consequences

The ship travelled from Hong Kong through East Asian ports, including Japan, and reached Vancouver, Canada, on 23 May 1914. It carried 376 passengers: 340 Sikhs, 24 Muslims and 12 Hindus. The passengers were British subjects of Indian origin, but Canadian officials prevented most of them from entering. Community supporters in Canada challenged the restrictions; the ship remained off Vancouver for about 2 months.

The ship was forced to leave Vancouver on 23 July 1914. It returned to India and reached Budge Budge, near Calcutta (now Kolkata), on 29 September 1914. A confrontation with British Indian authorities followed, during which passengers were killed and many were arrested. The tragedy sharpened anger at the unequal treatment of Indians across the British Empire.

How Ghadar and Komagata Maru were linked

The Ghadar Party did not charter Komagata Maru; Gurdit Singh did. However, Ghadar activists and supporters helped publicise the passengers' cause, and revolutionary literature reached people connected with the voyage. The refusal of entry in Canada and the violence following the return to India increased resentment against colonial rule. This is why Komagata Maru is studied alongside the Ghadar movement, although the two were not the same organisation or event.

Place the overseas movement in chronological order

The key sequence is 1905, Shyamji Krishna Varma's London institutions including India House; 1907, Madam Bhikaiji Cama's flag display at Stuttgart; 1913, the Ghadar Party and its newspaper on the U.S. Pacific Coast; 1914, Komagata Maru at Vancouver and Budge Budge; and 1914–1915, the unsuccessful Ghadar effort to organise revolt in India during World War I. These were linked by a common concern for India's freedom, not by a single unified command.

Prelims focus

  • Gurdit Singh chartered the Japanese ship Komagata Maru.
  • The ship reached Vancouver on 23 May 1914 carrying 376 Indian passengers.
  • Canada's continuous journey regulation dated from 1908.
  • The ship left Vancouver on 23 July 1914.
  • It reached Budge Budge near Calcutta on 29 September 1914, where a deadly confrontation followed.
  • Trap: Gurdit Singh organised the voyage; the Ghadar Party was not the ship's charterer.

[Sources: Parks Canada, The Komagata Maru Incident of 1914 National Historic Event, historical event account and plaque text, last updated 9 March 2023 (consulted 21 November 2026); Ministry of Culture, Government of India, Komagata Maru Incident, Press Information Bureau backgrounder, 29 September 2014 (consulted 21 November 2026); IGNOU, History of India VIII (c. 1857–1950), Unit 9, section 9.4, printed pp. 121–123; Government of Tamil Nadu, History, Class 12, Volume 1, Unit 3, printed p. 35.]
